label: Title
notes: Open by naming the source heading, Applications of Cohomology, while keeping the manifest title as the deck title. The aim is to make the chapter feel like one machine: Hirzebruch-Riemann-Roch computes an Euler characteristic, vanishing removes higher cohomology from that number, and Kodaira embedding uses the surviving sections to produce projective geometry. Keep the source grounding explicit: printed pages 231 through 254 and PDF pages 240 through 263.

label: Map of the Argument
notes: Use this as the mental table of contents for the hour. The first block belongs to printed pages 231 through 238, where Euler-Poincare characteristics, Chern characters, Todd classes, examples, the chi-y genus, and index-theorem language appear. The middle block belongs to pages 239 through 246, where positivity and Bochner-type identities produce Kodaira and projective-space vanishings. The final block belongs to pages 247 through 254, where the embedding theorem and torus projectivity criteria are consequences.

label: HRR Ledger
notes: Present HRR as bookkeeping with geometric content, not as a black-box miracle. The left side is an alternating cohomology count for a holomorphic vector bundle or coherent sheaf in the appropriate version; the right side is built from Chern data. Students should hear that lower-degree terms matter only through products that land in top degree. This is why the formula is effective in examples: the ledger discards everything except the degree matching the complex dimension.

label: Examples
notes: Move quickly through the examples as calibration points. On a curve, HRR reproduces the familiar Riemann-Roch expression, so students can recognize the new theorem inside an older formula. On a surface, the same mechanism becomes intersection theory because top degree is now degree four. For a complex torus, the tangent bundle is holomorphically trivial, so the Todd factor is trivial and the computation emphasizes how special the torus case is.

label: Chi-y Genus
notes: Frame the chi-y genus as a controlled way to combine many Euler characteristics at once. The exact specializations depend on the setting and conventions, but the instructional point is stable: the same characteristic-class technology sees different classical invariants when the parameter is evaluated. This prepares the audience for the broader index-theorem orientation that follows. Avoid turning the slide into a catalogue; keep it as a dashboard metaphor grounded in the chapter's treatment.

label: GRR Orientation
notes: This slide is for orientation rather than proof. Grothendieck-Riemann-Roch says the HRR ledger behaves correctly under maps once the right Todd corrections are included. The Atiyah-Singer comparison explains why an Euler characteristic of a sheaf can be read as the index of an elliptic operator. Students do not need the full analytic theorem here; they need to see that the chapter's formula belongs to a larger index-theoretic family.

label: Additivity
notes: Use the exact sequence slide to connect formal algebra with geometric examples. The key reason Euler characteristics are useful is that they are additive even when individual cohomology dimensions are not. The hypersurface sequence is the geometric model: the structure sheaf of a divisor is measured by subtracting a twisted ideal sheaf from the ambient structure sheaf. This supports later arguments where vanishing turns these ledger identities into actual section counts.

label: Positive Line Bundles
notes: This is the analytic entrance to the second part of the chapter. A holomorphic line bundle becomes positive when a Hermitian metric has positive curvature in the appropriate (1,1)-sense. Stress the change of scale: positivity is a pointwise tangent-space condition, but the consequences are global. The following slides explain the mechanism by which a curvature inequality forces cohomology groups to vanish and therefore lets HRR count sections.

label: Kodaira Vanishing
notes: State Kodaira vanishing in the form the chapter needs: positive L kills the higher cohomology of K_X tensor L. Then point back to HRR. Once the higher terms vanish, the Euler characteristic is no longer an alternating shadow; it is the actual dimension of H0. This is the decisive bridge from curvature to the existence of holomorphic sections. The (p,q) grid is only a visual scaffold for where the Bochner argument acts.

label: Nakano Identity
notes: Do not attempt a full analytic proof on this slide. Instead, identify the dependencies that make the proof work. The Kahler identities relate the Dolbeault Laplacian to curvature terms, and positivity gives the curvature term a sign. For a harmonic representative, the identity says a sum of nonnegative quantities is zero. The conclusion is that the representative vanishes, and Hodge theory then translates that analytic statement into cohomology vanishing.

label: Projective Space Vanishing
notes: Use projective space as the example students can calculate with their hands. Positive twists of the hyperplane bundle have sections represented by homogeneous polynomials, and the higher cohomology vanishes in the expected range. The slide also warns that vanishing is not simply a statement that all twists are easy; negative twists reappear at the top by duality. This example anchors the later projective embedding discussion in a familiar coordinate model.

label: Weak Lefschetz
notes: Treat Weak Lefschetz as another payoff of positivity and vanishing, not as a disconnected theorem. A smooth ample hypersurface is cohomologically close to the ambient manifold in a precise range: below the middle dimensions the restriction map preserves information, and at the boundary it remains injective. The range matters because it prevents overstatement. The pedagogical message is that ample divisors can test global topology while being lower-dimensional and often easier to understand.

label: Serre to Grothendieck
notes: Make this slide feel like a technique transfer. Serre vanishing says that after enough positive twisting, coherent sheaves behave as if higher cohomology is no longer obstructing global generation. On P1, this control is strong enough to feed the Grothendieck splitting lemma for vector bundles. The point is not to reprove the full splitting theorem, but to show how positivity, vanishing, and generation keep reappearing as a single method.

label: Linear Systems
notes: This is the practical criterion behind Kodaira embedding. First, basepoint freeness ensures the projective map is actually defined at every point. Second, point separation ensures two different points are not collapsed to the same projective coordinate vector. Third, tangent separation ensures the differential is injective, so the map is an immersion. Students should see that an embedding theorem is not magic; it is a checklist about sections and first-order data.

label: Blow-Up Bridge
notes: Explain why blow-ups appear in a proof about embeddings. Separating a point, a pair of points, or a tangent direction is a local condition, but Kodaira vanishing is a global theorem about line bundles. The blow-up converts the local condition into a statement involving an exceptional divisor. If the adjusted line bundle remains positive enough, vanishing gives the needed surjectivity of sections. This is the bridge from analytic positivity to the linear-system checklist.

label: Kodaira Embedding
notes: State the theorem in the positive-line-bundle form: if a compact complex manifold has a positive holomorphic line bundle, then a high tensor power has enough holomorphic sections to define a projective embedding. The proof flow is the chapter's synthesis. Positivity feeds Kodaira-type vanishing; vanishing gives surjectivity to local data; surjectivity gives basepoint, point, and tangent separation; those three tests turn the section map into an embedding.

label: Tori and Projectivity
notes: Use the torus criterion to separate Kahler geometry from algebraic geometry. Complex tori are naturally Kahler in many cases, but projectivity requires an integral positive class, expressed classically as a Riemann form on the lattice. The cone in the diagram represents positivity, while the lattice dots represent arithmetic integrality. Projectivity happens where the two conditions meet. This fits the chapter's larger theme: analytic positivity needs the right cohomological and integral packaging to become algebraic.

label: Closing Synthesis
notes: Close by returning to the chapter's governing promise. Divisors give line bundles, line bundles live in the Picard group, and positivity of those line bundles can force projective embeddings. Cohomology is the measuring device at every step: HRR computes Euler characteristics, vanishing removes the alternating ambiguity, and separation criteria interpret sections geometrically. Make clear that this lecture stops with the assigned Chapter 5 span and does not use the deformation material that begins at the end of PDF page 263.
